What it does

Tracks your walk on the Monon, snapped to the trail so GPS wobble doesn't pad your miles. A conductor calls every stop with a bit of history, times your splits, and knows when you've turned around.

The person waiting at home gets an arrivals board with where you are and when you’ll be home, and can send telegrams that the conductor reads aloud.

Who calls the stops?

Turn your sound on. The demo runs 30 times faster than a real walk.

A conductor for your walks on the Monon Trail, and an arrivals board for the person waiting at home. Set it up once.

The Monon Trail follows the old Monon Railroad line. The app knows it from 10th Street in Indianapolis, north through Broad Ripple, to 146th Street in Carmel.

Advanced: relay server

Leave blank to use ntfy.sh. A custom relay is written into the board link you send, so her board follows it.

Anyone with your board link can follow your walks. If it reaches someone it shouldn’t, make a new one: the old link stops following at once, even mid-walk.

Maps

Maps open on satellite pictures, which need no setup. The street map comes from CARTO, which now asks for a free key: get one at carto.com/basemaps/apikey, paste it here, and the arrivals board uses it too. Without a key the street choice shows a plain line map.

Backup

Walks live only on this phone. Save a backup file now and then, or before switching phones.

The file holds your home location, every walk with its route from your door, your named spots and your settings, so keep it somewhere private. It doesn’t hold your board link.

About

How it works

Tracking

GPS points are matched to the trail itself, so distance on the Monon is measured along the path and stray points get thrown out. Off the trail, points are smoothed before they count. The app knows the trail from 10th Street to 146th Street in Carmel, and any spots you name along it.

Phones pause web pages when the screen locks. Keep the screen on (the app asks for that) and use Pocket mode. If tracking does pause, the gap is measured along the trail when you come back.

Home time

The home estimate uses your recent pace, stops included, and the distance left: back along the trail, then the same way home you came. Before you turn around it assumes your chosen turnaround, then your usual one.

Put it on your phone

The preview inside Claude can't use GPS. Host the index.html file on any free static host, then add it to your Home Screen.

What's new

  • Trips: plan a walk to anywhere, like a gym downtown, by search or on the map, with stops of your own. The route rides the Monon when it helps, the conductor calls the turns and the Monon’s stations, and a new route comes if you leave this one.
  • If the phone pauses the conductor’s voice after a locked screen or a call, the app now wakes it and says the line again, so telegrams and the home-by warning still get through.
  • Making a new board link cuts off the old one at once, even in the middle of a walk, and the old board says the link was replaced.
  • The Depot is calmer: the Departures board and All aboard lead, and choices you set once, like the voice, fold away until you open them.
  • Setting up a new phone is easier: home can be picked on a map, the first turnaround makes a walk of about four miles, and the board link carries your name, so the board says whose walk it is from the first open.
Earlier updates
  • The Departures board reads the weather for the hours your walk takes, with the latest time to leave and still be home dry, or a nearer turnaround that is.
  • Race a ghost you can see: pick your best or your last walk to tonight’s turnaround, watch it on the map, and get the result on your ticket.
  • A recap ticket appears on the Depot when a month or season ends, the recap can step back through earlier ones, and December brings a year in review.
  • Telegrams and alerts now cut into a long story part between sentences, and the captions show times and distances as you would write them.
  • Maps keep showing in the trail’s weak spots: tiles along the trail stay on this phone, and Settings can save the whole trail for offline.
  • All aboard opens a ready check of GPS, sound, the live board, the screen and the battery. When everything is clear it departs after a two-second countdown, and Wait stops it. Settings can switch the check off.
  • Monon Chronicles tells the railroad’s story in eight chapters, a part every few minutes on your walks. Story so far replays any chapter you have heard.
  • The Ticket book’s Stats tab adds a calendar of your nights on the line, trail heat, segment times, and a recap of the month, season or year with a poster to share.
  • The Depot shows your walk from this night a month or a year ago, when there was one.
  • Tap any map to open it full screen: drag, pinch or scroll to explore, follow the walk live, tap a station for its sheet, and see a past walk’s pace in color.
  • Her board can switch to a full-screen station sign for a phone propped up at home, and keeps that screen awake while you walk.
  • Satellite view on every map, from Indiana’s statewide aerial photos, with station names along the line. The switch on each map flips to the street map.
  • On iPhone, setup points to the Home Screen icon first, and a backup carries your walks from Safari to the icon.
  • Alerts and the last update of a walk keep trying until they land, and the pickup card says whether her phone got the alert.
  • Heading home by the streets ends the walk at your door, and a pause no longer looks like a long stop.
  • Her board tells a walk that ended away from home apart from one that ended at home, and shows last night's walk as history.
  • Resuming a walk after a reload no longer reads old telegrams aloud, and an unfinished walk is saved before a new one starts.
  • A Departures board on the depot: tonight's turn, the round trip, and when you'd be home if you left now. All aboard stays in reach, and a home-by time gets a yes or a nearer stop.
  • A red enamel station sign, one instrument cluster, and clear On and Off controls in the cab. The sign says if you walk past your turnaround.
  • Pocket mode shows a countdown, a progress rail, her latest telegram and any check-in, in a red you can actually read.
  • Her board puts the telegram and the guess near the top, groups alerts in one card, and her intro sets up sounds and alerts.
  • Ticket book tabs and month headings, records that open their walk, and a share picture with a tear-off stub.
  • Four voices: Conductor, Coach, Historian and Night Owl, each with its own check-ins.
  • Weather, rain warnings, sunset and the moon phase, plus a Dispatch card before you leave.
  • A live map and a trip chart on the arrivals board, cheers she can send, and a heads-up time she picks.
  • A check-in after ten minutes stopped, with an alert to the board if there's no answer.
  • The whole Indianapolis trail from 10th Street, your own named spots, and a sheet for every stop.
  • Plan by distance or time, walk details with a route map, shareable ticket pictures, and weekly charts.
  • Retries when the signal drops, a custom relay option, backups, a first-walk checklist and a big view.
  • Race a ghost of your best walk, earn merit badges, get a Monday recap, and send quick replies from the cab.
  • Her board adds tonight's timeline, a guess-his-arrival game he hears about, and a QR code for the link.

Voices

Four voices share one brain. The Conductor calls stations with a bit of history. The Coach watches your pace, compares miles, and nudges you when you fade. The Historian tells more stories. The Night Owl keeps quiet, checks in every half hour, and mentions the moon and sky.

Weather and sky

Weather comes from Open-Meteo and refreshes every 30 minutes on a walk, with rain warnings when a shower looks likely within the hour. Sunset and the moon phase are calculated on this phone. The moon phase is the average cycle, so it can be off by up to a day.

Rain is likely when the forecast gives it a 50 percent chance or more in an hour, and a chance from 30 percent. Open-Meteo's 15-minute forecast times its start and end where it agrees with that, and otherwise the board gives the hour. Advice to beat the rain leaves ten minutes to spare. Wind chill and heat index use the formulas of the U.S. National Weather Service. Without a signal the board uses the last forecast for up to six hours, and says when it was made.

Privacy

Your walks, history and settings stay on this phone. These services see a little, and only when used. Each one sees this phone’s internet address when it is used:

  • ntfy.sh carries live board updates, encrypted on this phone first. The key lives only in the board link, so anyone with the link can follow your walks from your door, and send you telegrams: send it to one person. If it reaches anyone else, Make a new board link in Settings cuts the old one off at once. The relay can see when updates are sent, but not what they say. Phone alerts, if she turns them on, are plain text the relay can read: your first name, the walk’s status, times and the nearest cross street or landmark on the trail, never your exact position. Before you leave, the ready check asks the relay whether it is up, and sends nothing else.
  • Open-Meteo gets your location rounded to about a kilometer, for the weather on the Depot and during walks.
  • Indiana’s imagery service (on Esri’s ArcGIS cloud), with the U.S. Geological Survey as a backup, serves the satellite pictures and sees which part of town is on screen. Tiles inside a strip along the trail are kept on this phone, as you look at them or all at once with Save trail maps for offline, so the maps show where the signal is weak; tiles outside the strip are never kept. The strip follows the trail’s line and is the same for everyone. It reaches a few hundred meters either side in close-ups and farther in the overview maps, so if you live near the trail, some kept tiles show your street. The arrivals board keeps the tiles it shows the same way, on the watcher’s phone. Delete them in Settings, under Maps.
  • CARTO serves the street map pictures, only once you add a key, and sees which part of town is on screen. The arrivals board uses your key too.
  • OpenStreetMap Nominatim gets the address or place you type, only when you search for your home or a trip. For a trip search it also gets this app’s web address, which its rules ask for.
  • FOSSGIS’s routing services (OSRM at routing.openstreetmap.de, and Valhalla at valhalla1.openstreetmap.de when OSRM doesn’t answer) get where a trip starts, its stops and where it ends, only when you plan a trip or one needs a new route, along with this app’s web address, which their rules ask for.
  • Google Fonts serves the typefaces when they load.
  • Apple Maps or Google Maps gets your position only if the watcher taps one of the map links on the arrivals board.

Trail hours

Carmel posts its Monon Greenway, north of 96th Street, as open sunrise to sunset. The conductor mentions it when you reach 96th after dark.
